title: Horace and Fletcher Henderson, and Ellington as accompanist
summary: Dance compares Horace Henderson's piano with Fletcher's simple style. She relays Cootie Williams calling Ellington the greatest accompanist, and Humes agrees an accompanist must anticipate the singer.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: Well, now I'm going to ask you about different sort of people. I'm going to ask you about Horace Henderson and Fletcher. You know Horace was a good piano player.
Before you were really professional, isn't it?
Yes. You know, when Roy and Sprat, they worked with him.

You know, Horace could get over the key board and he had fairly on-going ideas for his day, you know, as compared with Fletcher who after all was something like Basie, played very simple things. But of course, he was sometimes a band pianist. He's not a guy that plays a whole lot of piano. I was talking to
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
Cootie (Williams) last week and he was saying to me that Ellington was the greatest accompanist in the world.
He said he never gets in your way. He always knows what you're going to do. He never ever gets in your way.
Well that's what the accompanist is all about.
